The rain began just after dawn, tapping first on the window ledge, then on the roof of the parked bicycle outside my door. I watched it turn the street into a long gray mirror, reflecting the pale glow of traffic lights that no one was obeying yet. A bus sighed at the corner, its breath fogging the glass, and a woman ran beneath an umbrella too small for the weather, clutching a paper bag as if it contained something fragile and important.

Inside my kitchen, the kettle clicked off. Steam rose in a thin ribbon, carrying the scent of tea leaves and old wood. I thought about how many mornings like this have passed without my noticing: ordinary hours folded quietly into memory, like letters placed inside envelopes and never sent. Yet there is comfort in such repetition. The world renews itself not with trumpets, but with small signals, bread warming, birds shifting from one wet branch to another, a neighbor’s radio murmuring through a wall.

I poured the tea and sat by the window. The rain continued, patient and unhurried, washing dust from the leaves of the maple tree in the yard. Somewhere beyond the rooftops, the city was waking, gathering its noise and urgency. But for now, in this narrow room, everything felt possible, even stillness. I drank slowly, listening to the rain rearrange the afternoon, and imagined all unseen gardens growing behind closed doors, waiting for sunlight that would arrive whether or not anyone remembered to look.
